result.summary: The Furies, furious at losing the trial of Orestes, threaten to poison the land of Athens. Athena patiently persuades them with promises of honour and a home, and they agree to bless the city instead.

scenes.title: The Chorus threatens Athens
scenes.summary: The Chorus laments its lost honour and threatens to blight the land. Athena warns them against excess and offers them honours and a home.
scenes.stakes: The Furies stand to lose their ancient honours; Athens is threatened with blight and sterility.

scenes.title: Athena pleads and warns
scenes.summary: The Chorus repeats its lament. Athena bears with their anger, asks them not to stir civil strife, and says they may stay or not, but must not harm the city.
scenes.stakes: The Furies fear dishonour beneath the earth; Athena seeks to protect her people from civil war and wrath.

scenes.title: The Chorus yields
scenes.summary: In quick exchanges Athena assures the Chorus of honour, power and a pledge. Their anger leaves them.
scenes.stakes: The Chorus risks being persuaded into a lesser place; Athena risks losing the chance to end the feud.

scenes.title: Blessings upon the city
scenes.summary: Athena tells the Chorus what blessings to invoke, and the Chorus promises them. Athena says the new divinities rule over mortal life.
scenes.stakes: The city's prosperity and the safety of its people depend on the goddesses' goodwill.

alias_notes.explanation: Pallas is a common epithet of Athena.

notable_quotes.reason: Athena states that she will not promise what she cannot fulfil.
Shows the Furies' new role as feared guardians of justice.

analysis.text: Persuasion replaces force: Athena wins the Furies over with promises, turning vengeance into a lasting civic blessing.
The play's ending honours Athenian law courts and warns against civil strife, speaking to Athens' political tensions in 458 BC.

fun_facts.text: After this scene the Furies are renamed Eumenides, 'the kindly ones', which gives the play its title.

language_notes.text: "Ridden down" means trampled over; the Furies accuse the Olympian gods of overriding the older, primal laws of blood-vengeance.
"Woe unto it" is a parenthetical cry; the Chorus pities the land even as it threatens it.
"Ah! just return!" is a parenthetical cry: the blight is called a just repayment for their lost honour.
"Canker" is a spreading disease or blight that destroys plants and living tissue.
Athena's claim to know the keys of Zeus's thunderbolt armoury recalls her place as his favourite daughter, born from his head.
"Froward" is archaic for wilful, contrary or unruly.
"Black billow" is a figure for the Furies' dark, surging anger, which Athena asks them to calm.
"Reft" is the old past tense of "reave": robbed or deprived. "Immemorial" means beyond memory, extremely ancient.
Erechtheus was an early legendary king of Athens. His house is the shrine on the Acropolis, where the Furies are promised a home.
"A fury not of wine" means a madness not caused by drink. Athena fears the Furies will inspire murderous quarrels among citizens.
"Birds' battling within the home" refers to cockfighting, an image for Athenians killing one another in civil war.
This sentence is garbled in this translation. Athena says she will keep offering her gifts so the elder goddess cannot claim a younger one dishonoured her; her persuasion may win the Furies over.
"Meed" is an archaic word for reward or due share; "full meed of honour" means the full honour deserved.
"What manner of abode" means what kind of dwelling; "thou sayest" is archaic second person singular.
"Votaries" are devoted worshippers; here, those who honour the Chorus with cult and sacrifice.
"Spells" here means persuasive, charming words, not literal magic. "Methinks" means "it seems to me."
Blessings that look to no 'evil victory' means prayers for a triumph that harms no one, such as one won through civil strife or injustice.
The speaker compares herself to a gardener tending a plant; 'stock' means the family line or breed of the just men.
Pallas is another name for Athena, used here by the Chorus.
'Burgeon' means to sprout or grow forth; 'propitious auguries' are favourable omens.
'Burghers' are citizens of the town; here, the people of Athens.
'Hale' means drag or haul; the sins of a man's ancestors drag him before the Furies for punishment.

context_notes.text: The Furies (Erinyes) are ancient goddesses of vengeance for blood-guilt. They are angry because Apollo and Athena have acquitted Orestes of his mother's murder.
The Furies are daughters of Night, so they belong to an older divine generation than the Olympians.
Athena offers them cult worship, with first-fruit offerings at births and weddings. This points to their later role as the Eumenides, the "Kindly Ones".
Night is the mother of the Furies in Aeschylus. They appeal to her as their primeval parent, older than the Olympian gods.
Athena concedes the Furies are older goddesses. Her respectful tone is part of her strategy of persuasion rather than force.
The Chorus are the Furies, goddesses of vengeance, now offered a shrine in Athens beneath the Areopagus after Orestes' acquittal.
Athena promises that Athenian households will need the Furies' favour to flourish, making them powerful guardians of prosperity.
The stage direction points to the audience, so the Athenian spectators are addressed as the 'just men'.
Ares was worshipped at Athens' Areopagus, 'hill of Ares', where the court that tried Orestes sits.
The Chorus, formerly the Furies, are now installed as Athenian divinities, the Eumenides or 'kindly ones', who oversee human fortune and punish wrongdoing.

literary_notes.text: Their wrath becomes venom dripping onto the soil, turning anger into a poison that sickens the land.
Blasted leaf and blasted child link crop failure with human infertility, making the threatened plague both agricultural and personal.
The Chorus's helpless question shows its anger giving way to uncertainty, and sets up Athena's persuasion.
Athena begins by flattering and denying their loss of honour, defusing their grievance before she asks for restraint.
Mentioning the thunderbolt while saying it is needless is a polite warning of the force behind her request.
Rage is imagined as a stormy sea that Athena asks the Furies to lull, as one might calm a child.
The Chorus addresses absent Night directly, calling on its mother to witness its suffering and lend authority to its complaint.
Athena mixes deference with quiet assertion of her own wisdom from Zeus, showing her as a tactful but authoritative mediator.
Plucking out the hearts of fighting-cocks stands for stirring citizens to brutal civil strife, turning people into aggressive birds.
The Chorus repeats its lament almost word for word, showing its stubborn grief and giving the scene a ritual, song-like rhythm.
The rapid line-by-line question and answer exchange, typical of Greek tragedy, quickens the pace as the Chorus's resistance gives way.
Athena presents herself as truthful and bound by her word, which gives her promise credibility and wins the Chorus's trust.
The Furies, once fierce and threatening, are softened by gentle words; persuasion succeeds where force would not, a central theme of the trilogy.
Athena likens her care for just men to a gardener nurturing plants, suggesting growth, protection and the weeding out of blight.
Whoever has never found the Furies grievous is ignorant of the true source of his sufferings, so his ease is itself a blindness.
Destruction acts like a silent, wrathful figure who levels the boaster, making ruin seem a patient, living power.
